Dear Mr.

In your letter of December 14, you ask me whether mathematics is a worthwhile endeavor. Mathematics absolutely is not a worthwhile endeavor! I can imagine only three possible reasons for studying mathematics:

(1) Entertainment.
(2) To promote technological progress.
(3) To promote one's own career.

Reason (1) is harmless; but one doesn't refer to entertainment as a "worthwhile endeavor"; it's just a pastime.

As for reason (2), modern technology is the worst thing that ever happened to the world, and to promote its progress is nothing short of criminal. Read Our Final Century, by Martin Rees; or read "Why the Future Doesn't Need Us", an article by Bill Joy that appeared in Wired magazine, April, 2000.

As for reason (3), to choose mathematics as one's career would be very risky. Not long ago I received a letter from a gravestone sculptor whose craft had been rendered obsolete by a laser-guided machine that carved gravestones automatically. He was in his forties, unable to find work, and depressed. Maybe you think that can't happen to you if you become a mathematician. But you're wrong. Martin Rees, Bill Joy, and many other distinguished experts believe that within a few decades machines will be developed that will be more intelligent than even the smartest human beings. When that happens, people will be obsolete; they will be phased out and will be replaced by computers and robots. This will happen to everyone eventually, but mathematicians probably will become obsolete before anyone else does, because mathematics is more amenable to computerization than any other field. Hence, computers probably will surpass humans in mathematics before they do so in other areas.

Sincerely yours,
Ted Kaczynski

NapMac is a drowsiness detection and focus app for Mac. It watches for the moment your eyes stay shut too long — and sounds the alarm before you fully drift off. Three built-in Pomodoro timers (25, 52, and 90 minutes) help you work in focused sprints, so you stay on task and alert. Powered by Apple's Vision framework and your Mac's built-in camera, it works entirely on-device. No video recorded, no data sent anywhere, no accounts needed. Just a quiet menu bar app that's got your back during long work sessions.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim liked to play
in his room with his toys. One day, he found a big box in his room.
Tim was very happy to see the box. He wanted to open it, but it was
difficult for him to open it.

Tim asked his friend, Sam, "Can you help me open the box?" Sam said,
"Yes, let's try together!" They tried to open the box, but it was
still hard. They were sad because they could not open it.

Then, Tim had an idea. He said, "Let's ask our friend, Mr. Fox, to
help us open the box." So, Tim and Sam asked Mr. Fox, "Can you help us
open the box?" Mr. Fox smiled and said, "Yes, I can help you."

Mr. Fox used his big nose to open the box. Inside, there were many
toys for Tim and Sam to play with. They were so happy and played with
the toys all day. They knew they could always count on each other to
help each other. And they lived happily ever after.

    It entirely omits consent, which would remain decisive even if every anatomical premise were granted.
    At absolute most, its premises make the fantasy not immediately self-contradictory. It leaps from “not ruled out by these fictional data” to “safe, desirable, and uniquely optimal.” That is an Olympic modal foul.

As rhetoric, though, it’s expertly engineered: grotesque conclusion, deadpan evidentiary voice, suspiciously specific numbers. Tavra should force every clause to close with fictional, questioned, or audibly inherited. 😂
